items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the plane region enclosed by the curve [MATH: y=\sqrt{x},] the curve [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x,] and the vertical line [MATH: x=2,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/412992e16c05a6566bedba04f7c272dd]

Content:
We rotate this region [MATH: 360^\circ] about the [MATH: x]-axis to get a solid of revolution, as shown below. How can we find the volume of this solid?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e85a3df0718cab6ff8f9965ef9ac69da]

Content:
To find the volume of the solid generated when the region bounded by the outer curve [MATH: y=f(x),] the inner curve [MATH: y=g(x),] and the vertical lines [MATH: x=a] and [MATH: x=b] is rotated [MATH: 360^\circ] about the [MATH: x]-axis, we use the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} \Big( \big[ \underbrace{f(x)}_\text{outer} \big]^2 - \big[ \underbrace{g(x)}_\text{inner} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
This method of computing the volume is called the washer method because it involves breaking up the region into many thin washers (one such washer is shown below).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fed3119bf984f02fc6d683e13451bf3f]

Content:
The cross-sectional area of each washer corresponds to the region between two discs of radius [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x),] so the area of each washer cross-section is

Content:
[MATH: \pi [f(x)]^2 - \pi [g(x)]^2,]

Content:
and this is what we integrate.

Content:
In our case, the outer curve is [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt{x}] and the inner curve is [MATH: g(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x,] so the volume is given by

Content:
[MATH: V = π∫_{0}^{2}(sqrt(x))^{2} − ((1)/(2)x)^{2}dx.]

Content:
which simplifies to
[MATH: V = π∫_{0}^{2}(x − (x^{2})/(4))dx.]

Content:
Evaluating this integral gives

Content:
[MATH: V|= π(∫_{0}^{2}xdx − (1)/(4)∫_{0}^{2}x^{2}dx); = π((x^{2})/(2)|_{0}^{2} − (1)/(4) ⋅ (x^{3})/(3)|_{0}^{2}); = π(((4)/(2) − 0) − (1)/(4)((8)/(3) − 0)); = π(2 − (2)/(3)); = (4π)/(3).]

Content:
So the volume of the solid is [MATH: \dfrac{4\pi}{3}] cubic units.

[IMG: /graphics/717f67720ed2bd6cb21b89fe23684b40]

Consider the region bounded by [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}] and [MATH: y=x^3,] as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated [MATH: 2\pi] radians about the [MATH: x]-axis.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt{x}] and [MATH: g(x)=x^3.]

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}] [MATH: f(x)|= g(x); sqrt(x)|= x^{3}; x|= x^{6}; x^{6} − x|= 0; x(x^{5} − 1)|= 0] Hence, the limits of integration are from [MATH: x=0] to [MATH: x=1.]

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner function [MATH: y=g(x)=x^3,] and

  • leaves through the outer function [MATH: y=f(x)=\sqrt{x}.]

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

[MATH: V|= π∫_{a}^{b}([outer]^{2} − [inner]^{2})dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}([sqrt(x)]^{2} − [x^{3}]^{2})dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}(x − x^{6})dx.]

sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/052083476ff31e9fbde6acb59b6a9ea2]

Consider the finite region bounded by [MATH: y=x^2] and [MATH: y=x^5,] as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated [MATH: 2\pi] radians about the [MATH: x]-axis.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: f(x)=x^2] and [MATH: g(x)=x^5.]

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f(x)|= g(x); x^{2}|= x^{5}; x^{5} − x^{2}|= 0; x^{2}(x^{3} − 1)|= 0] Hence, the limits of integration are from [MATH: x=0] to [MATH: x=1.]

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner function [MATH: y=g(x)=x^5,] and

  • leaves through the outer function [MATH: y=f(x)=x^2.]

Therefore, the volume is given by

[MATH: V|= π∫_{a}^{b}([outer]^{2} − [inner]^{2})dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}([x^{2}]^{2} − [x^{5}]^{2})dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}(x^{4} − x^{10})dx; = π((x^{5})/(5) − (x^{11})/(11))|_{0}^{1}; = π[((1)/(5) − (1)/(11)) − 0]; = (6π)/(55).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the plane region enclosed by the curve [MATH: y=\sqrt{x},] the curve [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x,] and the vertical line [MATH: x=2,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/412992e16c05a6566bedba04f7c272dd]

Content:
We rotate this region [MATH: 360^\circ] about the [MATH: x]-axis to get a solid of revolution, as shown below. How can we find the volume of this solid?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e85a3df0718cab6ff8f9965ef9ac69da]

Content:
To find the volume of the solid generated when the region bounded by the outer curve [MATH: y=f(x),] the inner curve [MATH: y=g(x),] and the vertical lines [MATH: x=a] and [MATH: x=b] is rotated [MATH: 360^\circ] about the [MATH: x]-axis, we use the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} \Big( \big[ \underbrace{f(x)}_\text{outer} \big]^2 - \big[ \underbrace{g(x)}_\text{inner} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
This method of computing the volume is called the washer method because it involves breaking up the region into many thin washers (one such washer is shown below).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fed3119bf984f02fc6d683e13451bf3f]

Content:
The cross-sectional area of each washer corresponds to the region between two discs of radius [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x),] so the area of each washer cross-section is

Content:
[MATH: \pi [f(x)]^2 - \pi [g(x)]^2,]

Content:
and this is what we integrate.

Content:
In our case, the outer curve is [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt{x}] and the inner curve is [MATH: g(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x,] so the volume is given by

Content:
[MATH: V = π∫_{0}^{2}(sqrt(x))^{2} − ((1)/(2)x)^{2}dx.]

Content:
which simplifies to
[MATH: V = π∫_{0}^{2}(x − (x^{2})/(4))dx.]

Content:
Evaluating this integral gives

Content:
[MATH: V|= π(∫_{0}^{2}xdx − (1)/(4)∫_{0}^{2}x^{2}dx); = π((x^{2})/(2)|_{0}^{2} − (1)/(4) ⋅ (x^{3})/(3)|_{0}^{2}); = π(((4)/(2) − 0) − (1)/(4)((8)/(3) − 0)); = π(2 − (2)/(3)); = (4π)/(3).]

Content:
So the volume of the solid is [MATH: \dfrac{4\pi}{3}] cubic units.

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About the X-Axis

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/717f67720ed2bd6cb21b89fe23684b40]

Consider the region bounded by [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}] and [MATH: y=x^3,] as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated [MATH: 2\pi] radians about the [MATH: x]-axis.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt{x}] and [MATH: g(x)=x^3.]

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f(x)|= g(x); sqrt(x)|= x^{3}; x|= x^{6}; x^{6} − x|= 0; x(x^{5} − 1)|= 0]
Hence, the limits of integration are from [MATH: x=0] to [MATH: x=1.]

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

[IMG: /graphics/377c31406bbd2d49601f4710ce71c3f9]

The vertical arrow

- enters the region through the inner function [MATH: y=g(x)=x^3,] and
- leaves through the outer function [MATH: y=f(x)=\sqrt{x}.]

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

[MATH: V|= π∫_{a}^{b}([outer]^{2} − [inner]^{2})dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}([sqrt(x)]^{2} − [x^{3}]^{2})dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}(x − x^{6})dx.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: f(x)=x^2] and [MATH: g(x)=x^5.]

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f(x)|= g(x); x^{2}|= x^{5}; x^{5} − x^{2}|= 0; x^{2}(x^{3} − 1)|= 0]
Hence, the limits of integration are from [MATH: x=0] to [MATH: x=1.]

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

[IMG: /graphics/a5f37789045f72a603b4307d34919b56]

The vertical arrow

- leaves through the outer function [MATH: y=f(x)=x^2.]

[IMG: /graphics/c5daedd33c9681519ec20ca7666d0377]

Content:
To find the volume of this solid, we can use the same washer method approach that we used earlier for the [MATH: x]-axis. The only difference is that we need to swap [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] in our formula.

Content:
So, to find the volume of the solid generated when the region bounded by the outer curve [MATH: x=f(y),] the inner curve [MATH: x=g(y),] and the horizontal lines [MATH: y=c] and [MATH: y=d] is rotated [MATH: 2\pi] radians about the [MATH: y]-axis, we use the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: V|= ∫_{c}^{d}π([f(y)_(⏟)_(outer)]^{2} − [g(y)_(⏟)_(inner)]^{2})dy.]

Content:
This is the same washer method as before, the only difference is that we need to swap [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.] It involves breaking up the region into many thin washers (one such washer is shown below).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2ad9bd30054d48d190b035dd0f7472b3]

Content:
The cross-sectional area of each washer corresponds to the region between two discs of radius [MATH: f(y)] and [MATH: g(y),] so the area of each washer cross-section is

Content:
[MATH: \pi [f(y)]^2 - \pi [g(y)]^2,]

Content:
and this is what we integrate.

Content:
In our example, the outer curve is [MATH: x=\sqrt{y}] and the inner curve is [MATH: x=y^2,] so the volume is given by

Content:
[MATH: V|= ∫_{0}^{1/2}π([sqrt(y)]^{2} − [y^{2}]^{2})dy.]

Content:
which simplifies to
[MATH: V|= π∫_{0}^{1/2}(y − y^{4})dy.]

Content:
Evaluating this integral gives

Content:
[MATH: V|= π(∫_{0}^{1/2}ydy − ∫_{0}^{1/2}y^{4}dy); = π((y^{2})/(2)|_{0}^{1/2} − (y^{5})/(5)|_{0}^{1/2}); = π(((1)/(8) − 0) − ((1)/(160) − 0)); = (19π)/(160).]

Item 9 — Example: Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About the Y-Axis

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/774fdf8f85e93bebd2f2e50488687ba6]

Consider the finite region bounded by [MATH: y=x^3] and [MATH: x=y,] where [MATH: y \leq 0,] as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated [MATH: 2\pi] radians about the [MATH: y]-axis.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Writing our first function in terms of [MATH: y,] we get
[MATH: y = x^{3}⟹x = root(y, 3).]

Let [MATH: f(y)=\sqrt[3]{y}] and [MATH: g(y)=y.]

Now, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f(y)|= g(y); root(y, 3)|= y; y|= y^{3}; y^{3} − y|= 0; y(y^{2} − 1)|= 0]

Hence [MATH: y=0] and [MATH: y=\pm 1.] But, since [MATH: y \leq 0,] the limits of integration are from [MATH: y=0] to [MATH: y=-1.]

Let's draw our horizontal arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

[IMG: /graphics/0a57cd58d6ef9de4e8fcb1bd7ddb2470]

The horizontal arrow

- enters the region through the inner function [MATH: x=g(y)=y,] and
- leaves through the outer function [MATH: x=f(y)=\sqrt[3]{y}.]

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

[MATH: V|= π∫_{a}^{b}([outer]^{2} − [inner]^{2})dy; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}([root(y, 3)]^{2} − [y]^{2})dy; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}(root(y^{2}, 3) − y^{2})dy.]

Item 12 — Example: Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About the Y-Axis

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/6966391c13faad4668ada923fcf2c17b]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: f(y)=\sqrt{4-y^2}\,] and [MATH: g(y)=1.]

Let's draw our horizontal arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

[IMG: /graphics/e73cee16d74035d7ce1f67f89adb1a4f]

The horizontal arrow

- enters the region through the inner function [MATH: x=g(y)=1,] and
- leaves through the outer function [MATH: x=f(y)=\sqrt{4-y^2}.]

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

[MATH: V|= π∫_{c}^{d}([outer]^{2} − [inner]^{2})dy; = π∫_{− 1}^{1}([sqrt(4 − y^{2})]^{2} − 1^{2})dy; = π∫_{− 1}^{1}(3 − y^{2})dy; = 2π∫_{0}^{1}(3 − y^{2})dy; = 2π(3y − (y^{3})/(3))|_{0}^{1}; = 2π(3 − (1)/(3) − 0); = (16π)/(3).]
